BLS Productivity Pipeline

US labour productivity time series from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and national population from Data USA, ingested and modelled on Databricks with Delta Lake, Unity Catalog and a Spark Declarative Pipeline.

github.com/gmatere/bls-productivity-pipeline

Source, PROCESS.md and the screenshots at full resolution.

13Files sourced
92,328Observations
337Series
11Tables in the pipeline

What it does

Pulls every file in the BLS pr/ time-series folder plus a national population API, lands them raw in a Unity Catalog Volume, then models them through Bronze, Silver and Gold to answer three questions. Re-running it changes nothing unless the source changed.

Eleven tables in one pipeline. Expectations sit on Silver.

Two decisions carry this submission. Q05 is the annual average rather than a fifth quarter, which changes the answer to question 2 — and a first-run bug produced empty tables while the pipeline reported success. Both are on the Decisions page.

Overview / Sourcing & idempotency

Step 1

Sourcing

Re-running must handle files that were added, changed or removed, and must not reprocess anything already ingested. Filenames can't carry that, because pr.data.0.Current changes in place.

Getting past the 403

BLS returns 403 to anonymous clients. Their access policy says they may block robots that don't identify themselves, so the fix is the one the policy asks for: a User-Agent carrying a contact address. That is following the rule, not getting around it.

Requests retry with exponential backoff — five attempts from 1.5s to 24s, on 429 and 5xx, honouring Retry-After. BLS almost certainly won't rate-limit thirteen requests, but a public endpoint deserves a polite client and a brief outage shouldn't fail the run.

The file list is read from the directory page at runtime. Nothing is hardcoded, so a file BLS adds tomorrow is picked up without a code change.

The manifest

One Delta row per file, holding its ETag, Last-Modified, SHA-256, size and status.

One file, one pass. The cheap check first, the authoritative one only when needed.

The headers are a hint; the hash is the proof. BLS builds its ETag from the publish batch rather than the file contents — pr.data.1.AllData and pr.series came back with the identical ETag "0d4ccef9f3bdd1:0". A republish therefore moves the ETag on files that didn't change, and the hash check is what stops the whole batch being downloaded again for nothing.

Removed files are marked, not deleted — a file disappearing upstream is worth knowing about, and deleting the row throws that away.

The tombstone pass assumed a single source. It compared the whole manifest against the BLS listing, which marked population.json removed on every run — it comes from the API and was never in that listing. Now scoped to rows whose source_url belongs to BLS. A manifest covering more than one source has to know which source each row came from.

Overview / Bronze / Silver / Gold

Step 2

Modelling

Bronze, Silver and Gold as a single Spark Declarative Pipeline, with expectations enforcing schema and key integrity on the way in.

LayerJob
BronzeStores what the source sent, everything as text, one table per file. Only names are cleaned — BLS pads its headers to fixed width inside a tab-separated file, so Spark can't resolve series_id at all, and Delta rejects the space in the API's Nation ID. Values pass through untouched.
SilverTrims, types and asserts. The series_id values are padded too — without trimming, WHERE series_id = 'PRS30006032' returns nothing and question 3 quietly has no answer. Types are cast on purpose rather than guessed. Expectations live here because this is the first layer that makes a claim about the data.
GoldOne table per question, nothing else.

SQL or PySpark

PySpark is primary and builds the Gold tables; Spark SQL is the documented alternative. They don't merely look alike — the SQL file full-outer-joins its result for question 2 against the PySpark Gold table and counts the rows that disagree.

SELECT count(*) AS mismatches
FROM sql_version s
FULL OUTER JOIN workspace.rearc.gold_series_best_year g USING (series_id)
WHERE s.year IS DISTINCT FROM g.year
   OR s.summed_value IS DISTINCT FROM g.summed_value;

mismatches
0

PySpark is primary because everything else is Python — the ingestion, the TSV reader, the expectations — and question 2's window function is easier to write there. SQL is clearer for plain aggregation: question 1 in SQL is four lines and needs no explanation. On a team where analysts contribute I'd flip the default.

Overview / The three answers

Gold layer

The three answers

1 · US population, 2013–2018

322,069,808Mean
4,158,441Std dev — sample
3,796,120Std dev — population
6Years observed

The question doesn't say which standard deviation. Spark's stddev returns the sample form, but 2013–2018 is the complete set of years the question names rather than a sample from a wider population — so the population form is arguably the better default. Both are emitted and the reader chooses.

2 · Best year per series

283Series with a best year
337Series in the metadata
54With no quarterly rows
Q05Excluded — annual average

Each row carries BLS's own series_title, so a reader unfamiliar with the codes can tell Employment for the Manufacturing sector, Index (2017=100) from …, Level (Millions of jobs). The 54 missing series exist in pr.series but carry no non-Q05 observations, verified by left-anti join.

3 · PRS30006032, Q01, with population

39Observation years, 1988–2026
11With a population figure
2020Missing from the API

The question asks for population where available, so this is a left join: observations run from 1988, the population API covers 2013–2019 and 2021–2024. The gap at 2020 is real — ACS published no 1-year estimate that year. Dropping the unmatched years would answer a different question.

Overview / Decisions & trade-offs

What was hardest

Decisions & trade-offs

The full write-up is in PROCESS.md. These are the four that changed an answer or nearly shipped a defect.

Q05 is the annual average, not a fifth quarter. pr.period lists Q01–Q04 as quarters and Q05 as AN AV. Question 2 asks for the largest sum "across all its quarters" — and including Q05 adds the average of four numbers to those same four numbers. Excluded, and carried through Silver as is_annual_average so the decision is visible where it's made rather than buried in a filter.

A green pipeline that produced nothing

dlt.read() reads the last committed version of a table, not the one being built in the current run. On a clean run every Silver table read an empty Bronze, produced zero rows, and the pipeline reported success. silver_population hid it, because its Bronze happened to exist from an earlier attempt — so only some tables were empty, which looked like a data problem rather than a framework one.

It only happens on a first run and fixes itself on the second, which is what makes it dangerous. I could have shipped this, watched it work every time I ran it, and handed over something that produces empty Gold tables for anyone deploying it fresh.

Does it work on a clean deployment is a different question from does it work. And a green pipeline with empty tables is worse than a failed one, because nothing tells you to look.

The label BLS had already written

A label composed from sector and measure rendered four different series identically. They differ by duration_code — percent change on the year, percent change on the quarter, an index, a level in millions of jobs — which that label threw away. pr.series carries a series_title that distinguishes them properly. I'd read enough of the documentation to find the lookup tables and not enough to notice the answer was in the file I already had open.

It surfaced because I looked at the rows rather than the row count. 283 labelled series is a number that looks correct whether or not the labels mean anything.

The deduplication that wasn't added

There are no duplicates on (series_id, year, period) across all 92,328 rows. That's asserted with an expectation rather than papered over with a dropDuplicates(), which on a pair with differing values picks one at random and produces a wrong number with nothing to warn you.

Deduplication belongs where duplicates are expected — at-least-once streaming, CDC replay — with a rule for which row wins. A transform that does nothing is worse than none at all, because it looks like a safety check and isn't one.

Trade-offs for a real client

Topic
Schema driftExpectations stop the run rather than dropping rows. The file count is deliberately not asserted — that would contradict handling files being added or removed — so it logs a warning. Next: a written contract per file, versioned with the code.
Data volumeThe whole folder is ~4 MB. No partitioning, no Z-ordering, no incremental read, because at this size they'd do nothing. At 100×: Auto Loader over the Volume, Silver incremental on a scan date, lookups unchanged.
CostThe manifest isn't a cost saving here and I won't pretend it is. Serverless on a triggered pipeline is right — seconds of work, on demand. For a real client: attribution before optimisation, because a cost nobody owns is a cost nobody reduces.
Access controlA read-only analyst gets SELECT on the three Gold tables and nothing else — no Bronze, no Silver, no Volume, no manifest. Free Edition is single-user so the grants are untested against a real second identity, which the write-up says plainly.
MonitoringExpectation pass rates first. The manifest second: a run where every file is skipped is normal for a monthly release and a problem if it persists past a publication date. The gap: a check that each Silver table has more than zero rows.
